title: Biblical and rabbinic
hook: laws from the Torah and laws from the rabbis carry different weight

segments.voice: Yesterday, seyag, and your line: a fence around the law. Did your small fence hold? Fences are rules the sages built. Today, how the law tells a fence from what it guards. Day one thousand one hundred ten.

On each night of Hanukkah, before the candles are lit, a blessing is said. It thanks God, who made us holy with commandments and commanded us to light the Hanukkah light. Commanded us. Here's the puzzle. Open the Torah from beginning to end and you won't find Hanukkah in it. The story belongs to a much later time. So where exactly did God command it? The Talmud asks that very question, out loud, in tractate Shabbat. The answer opens up a distinction Jewish law leans on quietly, day after day. Today's word is one half of it.
screen: `WHO COMMANDED US TO LIGHT.` → `NO HANUKKAH IN THE TORAH.` → `SO WHERE WAS IT COMMANDED?`

segments.voice: D'oraita. It's an Aramaic word meaning from the Torah, and it names a law that comes from the Torah itself. Its partner is d'rabbanan, from the rabbis: a law the sages set. Start with the difference in source. Keeping the Sabbath, eating matzah on the first night of Passover: the Talmud treats these as d'oraita, from the verses. Lighting Hanukkah candles, many of the fences you met yesterday: d'rabbanan. Second, the puzzle. If Hanukkah is rabbinic, how can the blessing say God commanded us? The Talmud gives two answers, from two sages. One points to Deuteronomy, where the people are told not to turn aside from what the judges of their day teach them. The other points to a verse in the Song of Moses: ask your father, and he will tell you; your elders, and they will say. Either way, the rabbis' rulings carry authority because the Torah itself sends people to their teachers. Rabbinic law isn't a stranger. It's a command to listen. Third, the weights really are different, and you can see it when things are unclear. The Talmud's working rule: when you're in doubt about a Torah law, lean strict. When you're in doubt about a rabbinic law, you may lean lenient. Same question, different weight. Fourth, why it matters on an ordinary day. Knowing the source tells you how to act when life gets messy: when you're unsure, when there's illness, when two duties collide. A rule's weight depends on where it came from. Different weights.
screen: `FROM THE TORAH, FROM THE RABBIS.` · `WHERE WERE WE COMMANDED?` · `IN DOUBT: STRICT, OR LENIENT.` · `THE SOURCE SETS THE WEIGHT.` · then, large: `DIFFERENT WEIGHTS.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is sorting one rule by its source. Settle, and breathe. Pick a rule in your own life. A household rule, a work policy, a promise you keep, a habit you treat like a law. Now ask where it comes from. Is it something you hold as basic, close to the ground of who you are? Or is it a fence you, or someone else, added later to protect that? Set it on one side or the other. Then notice: if you were unsure about it, would you lean strict, or lean easy? The bell holds the time.
D'oraita. Aramaic for from the Torah: a law that comes from the Torah itself, set beside d'rabbanan, a law from the rabbis. Today's word.
Your line: different weights. Today, when two obligations pull at you, ask which one is the ground and which one is the fence, and give each its own weight. Day one thousand one hundred ten.

howItsDone: When a rabbi answers a question of Jewish law, the source of the rule matters: a doubt about a Torah law is usually resolved strictly, and a doubt about a rabbinic law may be resolved leniently. The Hanukkah blessing is said over a rabbinic command.
